answer.summary: Pfeffer argues that breaking conventional rules can make you memorable and help you stand out from people or businesses following norms that often favor incumbents. The useful departures are those that play to your strengths and improve your chances of success.

sections.heading: Why it can build power
sections.content: Doing something unexpected makes you stand out and become memorable. Pfeffer also notes that rules are often made by people favored by the existing arrangement, so doing things differently can disrupt incumbents and create an advantage.

sections.heading: What it can look like
sections.content: In business, Pfeffer points to Southwest Airlines not using the hub-and-spoke model, Amazon emphasizing exceptional customer service, and Whole Foods fitting local tastes rather than optimizing store costs. For an individual, he says to choose departures from convention that play to your strengths, help you stand out, and make you more successful. One example is asking for help despite the convention that you should demonstrate self-sufficiency.

sections.heading: Example of a person defying norms
sections.content: Pfeffer describes investor Jason Calacanis as defying venture-capital conventions: making many small bets rather than a few large ones, running a lean operation, and having no partners. Pfeffer also connects Calacanis’s journalism background—asking smart people questions—to developing insight into the internet industry.

judgment.explanation: The answer covers both reasons Pfeffer gives: unconventional behavior makes someone stand out and memorable, and existing rules often favor those who benefit from the status quo, so doing things differently can disrupt incumbents. Its examples and added details are supported by the cited context.
